entries.title: The Cop Who Took On Flock
entries.summary: After Noel Pichardo called out his city's embrace of Flock surveillance cameras, he was subjected to five internal affairs investigations in less than two years.
entries.content:
On an early fall afternoon in 2023, midway through a shift in Pawtucket’s District Five, Rhode Island police officer Noel Pichardo noticed a strange camera perched on a utility pole over West Avenue.

Pichardo was 28, five years into the job, and alone in his cruiser during one of the brief lulls between responding to the typical churn of radio calls for domestic disputes, petty disturbances, and welfare checks. The camera was compact and solar-powered, angled down toward passing traffic. Pichardo made a U-turn and drove beneath it again, more slowly this time, to get a better look.

He then began searching for the cameras on roads near highway ramps, at major intersections, along the routes into and out of the city. He found them again and again. By the time Pichardo finished circling the district, he knew exactly where he had seen them before.

Two years earlier, officers had gathered on the second floor of a small police substation in Pawtucket for a presentation about a surveillance system made by Flock Safety. A high-ranking police official stood in front of a PowerPoint and explained that the company’s automatic license plate readers could identify passing vehicles not only by their license plates but by bumper stickers, roof racks, and other distinguishing features. Investigators could search for a particular car across jurisdictions and, camera by camera, reconstruct where it had been.

The system was presented as another tool of routine police work, a way to recover stolen cars, locate suspects, and find missing people. But as Pichardo listened, he found himself thinking less about the vehicles police wanted than about all the others. In a medium-size city like Pawtucket, where a handful of roads carried people nearly everywhere they needed to go, a record of a car’s movements amounted to a record of a person’s life—the places they visited, the people they saw, the routines they followed.

As Pichardo understood it, the Flock proposal had gone nowhere because the city could not afford a permanent installation. So he let it slip from his mind.

But now, on that afternoon on West Avenue, the cameras were all over his district.

Pawtucket’s cameras are one small piece of a sprawling vehicle-surveillance system that touches nearly every state in the country. Flock markets its platform as the nation’s largest fixed license-plate-reader network, processing billions of sightings each month. Because departments can open their records to agencies elsewhere, a camera installed by one municipality can become searchable by investigators hundreds or thousands of miles away.

In 2021, around the time of Pichardo’s training, Flock offered Pawtucket police a free 60-day pilot. Seventeen cameras went up around the city as part of a regional test that also included Cranston and Woonsocket, according to records reviewed by WIRED. The rollout quickly drew criticism. The ACLU of Rhode Island accused the department of installing the cameras surreptitiously, after the pilot began without prior public input or notice to the city council. Pawtucket chief of police Tina Goncalves later apologized, saying that the department would “work better in the future” to communicate with the city council.

The pilot ended later that year, and in May 2023 the local TV news reported that Pawtucket was not moving forward with the installation. Pichardo believed the idea was a dead letter.

It was not. In September 2023, records show, Pawtucket moved forward with a two-year deployment worth $128,000. Records show that the city planned to install 20 cameras along many of its busiest roads, including Newport Avenue, Main Street, Broadway, Smithfield Avenue, and West Avenue—where Pichardo first noticed one hanging over the road.

“Wait a minute,” Pichardo recalled thinking. “When did we make this decision to put these up?”

Within months, Pichardo’s questions would set off a chain of events that, he says, ended his career in law enforcement. They would also eventually place him, somewhat improbably, at the center of a backlash against Flock that unites large factions of the American left and right.

For a policeman, Pichardo contains more than his share of contradictions. He speaks with a thick Rhode Island accent that sounds like something lifted from a cop movie, but he peppers his conversation with occasional references to Nietzsche or obscure films. He describes himself as private by temperament but seems driven to stand out.

Having spent some of his childhood in a poor neighborhood where drugs and gangs were part of the landscape, Pichardo says he learned that it was safest to keep his opinions to himself and stay out of other people’s business. When he was 12 or 13, he learned that his father, who had returned to the Dominican Republic several years earlier, had done so because he had a criminal record and was told it would be best if he left the country. Becoming a police officer offered a way of drawing a line between his father’s path and his own. After studying in the criminal justice program at Salve Regina University in Newport, Pichardo entered the police academy and joined the Pawtucket department in 2018. To hear him describe it, he’s always been something of an outlier on the force. “I’m possibly the only cop who would voluntarily go to musicals,” he once told me.

In the weeks following that fall shift when he first noticed Flock cameras all over town, Pichardo kept picking at the question of how the cameras had returned. Detectives, he says he learned after asking around the department, were already using the system, though many patrol officers like himself appeared to know little about it.

Pichardo contacted his work district’s local city council rep and asked how the cameras had been approved—his first time speaking to a politician, he says—but didn’t emerge with a clear answer. (Records show that the department had notified the purchasing board that it planned to move forward, but there was no public vote before the cameras were installed. The question of approval surfaced only afterward, when a council member asked whether the deployment should have come before the council. Officials said no. Installing the cameras was, they explained, an “administrative prerogative.”)

Police officers swear oaths to uphold the law and report wrongdoing. Inside the department, Pichardo said, the unwritten rule was simpler: Don’t rat. He understood that speaking publicly could end his career. But he says he was inspired by whistleblowers like Frank Serpico and Edward Snowden, men of conviction who broke with powerful institutions and spent years living with the consequences. Pichardo has a pronounced sense of right and wrong and a tendency to treat compromise as betrayal. “You should never sell your integrity,” he says.

License plate readers are a routine investigative tool, useful for locating stolen cars or identifying suspect vehicles without stopping large numbers of motorists. Experts broadly agree that reducing unnecessary police encounters and high-speed pursuits is a good thing. But to Pichardo, that usefulness was beside the larger point. Pawtucket had created a new form of surveillance over public movement with no debate, helping to build a world in which the government could quietly record where ordinary people went. It was not a world he found acceptable. If the officers who understood the system would not raise that question, he wondered, who would?

Pichardo was still wrestling with whether to speak out about Flock when he brought it up with his wife, Emily. “Do what you believe is right,” she said; they would deal with whatever followed. After that, without notifying anyone in the department, Pichardo called a reporter at Pawtucket’s local newspaper.

The article in the Valley Breeze was published on October 11, 2023. Its headline was blunt: “Pawtucket Officer Has a Big Problem With New Cameras.”

In the article, Pichardo called Flock a “grave threat” to privacy and warned that the system was ripe for abuse. He said he had learned of the full deployment from the newspaper itself, not from his own department. If a patrol officer knew so little about the cameras going up around the city, he asked, how much could the public possibly know? The whole thing gave him, he said, “1984 vibes.”

This was not whistleblowing in the conventional sense. Pichardo did not reveal a secret program, leak internal documents, or expose a specific abuse. In some respects, the newspaper knew more about the deployment than he did. What he offered instead was the rare perspective of an active-duty police officer breaking ranks to publicly argue that his own department had adopted a powerful surveillance system without enough scrutiny.

When the article appeared, the first text Pichardo received came from another officer.

“I want to congratulate you on your testicular fortitude,” it read. The officer added that he was proud of Pichardo for doing what he believed was right. Then he warned him: The brass was furious.

Pichardo says many officers supported what he had said to the Valley Breeze. Others, mostly older officers, viewed him as a traitor. One officer asked how he still had a job. Around the station, he was told that officers were calling him “Valley Breeze” behind his back. One sergeant, he says, told him he should quit.

Within weeks, the warnings began to look prescient.

Police internal investigations are not criminal cases. Their purpose is generally narrower—to determine whether an officer has violated a policy, code of conduct, or general order. Investigators interview witnesses, review body-camera or surveillance footage, collect reports and emails, and question the officer at the center of the complaint. The interview is typically recorded, and the officer is often accompanied by a union representative.

The process generates paper. A complaint. A notice of investigation. Lists of possible policy violations. Interview recordings and investigators’ notes. Findings, disciplinary recommendations, and notices of punishment.

Before the Valley Breeze article appeared, Pichardo’s disciplinary record appears to have consisted of a single incident: In 2021, while working a police detail at a production of the musical Annie, he refused a vendor’s request that he wear a face mask, and he received a written reprimand and a two-week suspension. After Pichardo spoke out against Flock, he received notice of an internal investigation into his conduct on October 25, 2023. It would be the first of many.

The department’s complaint, which originated from Chief Tina Goncalves, stated flatly that Pichardo had spoken to a newspaper without prior authorization, had undermined the authority of the police department and its chief, and had suggested that information collected by Flock cameras could be used improperly. His comments, the notice said, were “liable to cause harm to the reputation of the department and affect the impact on the community.”

The potential violations included the department’s mission statement, code of ethics, media-relations policy, and a rule labeled “Criticism & Malicious Gossip.”

Pichardo was ordered to appear at the Office of Professional Standards, a basement-level room in the Pawtucket police headquarters. Across from him, he says, were a lieutenant and a sergeant. A union representative sat beside him but said little.

The interview lasted somewhere between 30 and 45 minutes, Pichardo recalls. The questions were straightforward at first. Had he spoken to the reporter? He had. Had he done so without authorization from the department? He had. Why?

Pichardo gave much the same answer he had given the newspaper: The cameras were tracking people across the city, and the public had a right to know how they were being used. Pichardo says the lieutenant disagreed. Not every police tactic, he told Pichardo, was the public’s business. Departments did not disclose every method they used or every form of surveillance available to them.

The investigators accused Pichardo of violating the public’s trust by speaking to the press.

“I think this department violated the public trust,” he says he retorted. Then they asked who, in his view, should be held responsible. “The chief,” Pichardo said.

WIRED could not review the underlying investigative file, including the recording that might confirm or contradict Pichardo’s account. The city declined to provide the file even when Pichardo requested records concerning his own case. Pawtucket officials did not respond to WIRED’s questions about the denial.

A disciplinary agreement signed in early 2024 does, however, state that Pichardo made “critical statements to the media” about Flock and the department’s leadership. Pichardo maintained that his comments were constitutionally protected speech. The department expressly denied that position in the agreement.

After consulting an attorney, the Pawtucket police union came to the conclusion that Pichardo’s comments were constitutionally protected and sent the city a letter warning that if it disciplined him, it would likely violate his rights. According to union lodge president Michael Cioe, the department initially sought a six-month suspension but reduced the proposed punishment after the union threatened litigation.

Rather than fight the case through disciplinary hearings and possible state or federal litigation, the two sides reached an agreement. Pichardo would serve a 30-day unpaid suspension for speaking to the paper.

Pichardo said he accepted the deal because he didn’t want his coworkers to see him as their enemy. “I wanted the war to end,” he says.

By then, the department had already opened another investigation into his conduct.

A month after investigators questioned Pichardo about speaking to the Valley Breeze, another internal investigation notice arrived. In December, the department opened an inquiry over Pichardo’s failure to appear for a municipal court hearing about a traffic citation, which resulted in an additional two-day suspension. Chief Goncalves was again listed as the complainant.

Then, in March, about a week after he returned to work from the suspension, yet another notice landed—this one concerning an encounter that had allegedly taken place nearly 15 months earlier.

The incident involved a man who was being taken to a hospital for a mental health evaluation. The complaint alleged that Pichardo grabbed the man’s arm, refused to let him retrieve a jacket, and would not allow him to feed his cat. When the man pointed out that the cat could not open a can of food on its own, Pichardo allegedly replied that “cats can take care of themselves” and laughed.

During his interview, Pichardo says he told investigators that the cat already had food and that other officers and mental health clinicians present could confirm that he had handled the encounter appropriately. Pichardo says the inquiry didn’t sustain the allegations, and he received no discipline.

By the spring, Pichardo felt sure that the department was trying to send a message with these three investigations. Inside the department, Pichardo says, there was an unspoken expectation that his disciplinary agreement with his superiors would end his public criticism. Nevertheless, in April he accepted an invitation to testify at a public hearing before the Rhode Island House Judiciary Committee, where lawmakers were considering legislation regulating automated license plate readers.

The hearing was carried live on the legislature’s Capitol Television network. Pichardo spoke off the cuff. He told lawmakers that the proposed legislation did not go far enough. Flock, he argued, was tracking people’s movements, and although he was “not a lawyer,” he believed the system raised serious Fourth Amendment concerns. He said the cameras had captured his own plate five times in a single day, cited an out-of-state officer who used Flock to track his ex-wife, and questioned whether police should possess technology with that kind of cross-jurisdictional reach.

At times, Pichardo’s confidence outran his precision. He asserted that officers’ use of Flock could not be monitored, although the system does in fact maintain user logs and performs regular audits. In interviews with WIRED, he acknowledged the distinction but argued that logs were only as meaningful as the people responsible for reviewing them. He pointed to cases in other jurisdictions where officers had used Flock to track romantic partners or conduct improper searches, sometimes without the misuse being caught until much later. His broader point, he said, was that “anybody’s capable of anything” when given a powerful tool without sufficient guardrails.

About a week later, in response to his testimony, the Rhode Island Police Chiefs’ Association sent a letter to the committee singling Pichardo out by name. It called his testimony “inaccurate at best” and, at worst, “inflammatory and patently false.” The association accused him of misunderstanding Flock’s capabilities, disputed his description of the system’s auditing, and suggested that he either lacked familiarity with the technology or had “an agenda where, in his mind, the truth is irrelevant.”

Back at work, Pichardo says, his union representatives were annoyed that he’d spoken up again. (The union disputes this characterization.) Other officers, even those who largely agreed with him about Flock, or at least respected what he was doing, started to express concerns. One sat Pichardo down and said that if he wasn’t careful, he might lose his job and never work as a police officer in Rhode Island again. “You’ve got to think about your family, dude,” Pichardo recalls him saying.

On May 10, 2024, a new incident set yet another internal investigation of Pichardo in motion: A delivery driver came to Pawtucket police headquarters to report that someone had thrown a bottle of soda at her vehicle during what she described as a road-rage encounter. Pichardo spoke with her, concluded that no crime had occurred, and declined to prepare a report.

The woman later spoke with a sergeant, asking for the incident to be documented, and Pichardo was directed to write a report. According to the department's records, the delivery driver was not initially asking to file a formal complaint against Pichardo, but she did return to the station later that day, recording portions of her exchanges with Pichardo on her cell phone.

Pichardo told her that Pawtucket is an urban environment where people argue and throw things, accused her of acting like a child and having a tantrum, and complained that she had “won” by persuading a supervisor to overrule him.

Several days later, the woman filed a formal complaint with the Office of Professional Standards.

Investigators reviewed the recordings and interviewed another officer on duty. The videos, investigators later wrote, showed the woman remaining largely calm as Pichardo became increasingly dismissive. They sustained more than a dozen allegations, including neglect of duty, insubordination, incivility, and conduct unbecoming.

Pichardo acknowledged to WIRED that his conduct was indefensible. “I should still be the bigger person,” he said.

What he disputed was the punishment: a 40-day unpaid suspension and removal from the detective eligibility list. He also says the union told him he was barred from taking the sergeant’s exam for two years. He was notified of the suspension on the day his second son was born, just as he was about to start paternity leave, meaning that his first 40 days at home with his baby were unpaid—a coincidence he alleges was deliberate.

By early 2025, Pichardo had come to believe the department was finished with him. He no longer trusted that, if a traffic stop, arrest, or routine encounter generated another complaint, anyone in command would give him the benefit of the doubt. He more or less began to avoid active patrolling, he says. Between calls, he often waited at the Fraternal Order of Police building, which he helped maintain, or remained inside his patrol car rather than looking for the next stop. “I was trying to stay off the radar,” he later recalled telling investigators.

Then two more investigations arrived.

The first grew out of a dispute over a snowbound Volkswagen. On February 10, Pichardo responded to what appeared to be an unregistered vehicle stranded in the snow, concluded it was already disabled and had been ticketed, and gave the owner until the following day to move it. A supervisor ordered him to return and have the car towed instead. Pichardo questioned the instruction over the radio before complying. The department concluded that he had essentially been insubordinate.

The second began less than two weeks later. Pichardo responded to a mother who wanted police to document her 13-year-old son as a wayward child after she suspected he had been burning paper inside their home. Pichardo declined to take a report, concluding that she lacked evidence and appeared more interested in having the state remove the boy than documenting a crime. Before leaving, he told her to go inside and “be a mother.”

The department combined the investigations. Rather than focus only on the underlying incidents, investigators reconstructed nearly an entire workday of Pichardo’s life in excruciating detail. Using dispatch records, time sheets, cruiser GPS, and location data transmitted by Pichardo's body camera, they mapped his movements throughout the day of the family call. (They didn’t use Flock data; they didn’t need to.) Their reconstruction concluded that he had spent approximately four hours and 57 minutes at police facilities or the Fraternal Order of Police building rather than on patrol.

Pichardo did not dispute where he had been. He explained that he helped maintain the union office and that officers routinely waited there between calls. From the department's perspective, the location data showed an officer spending much of his shift inside police or union buildings instead of policing the city. The department was recommending termination. The resulting complaint explaining the decision ran 25 pages. It contained 32 administrative charges—10 stemming from the tow dispute and 22 from the family call—and assembled nearly every disciplinary matter from Pichardo's career.

On the morning of July 16, 2025, after roll call, a major asked Pichardo to stay behind.

He knew what was coming.

Chief Goncalves had signed a complaint the day before recommending his termination. The major handed it to him and explained that he was being suspended with pay while he decided whether to request a hearing in accordance with Rhode Island's Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. He had five days.

Pichardo took the complaint home. But the more he thought about it, the less sense it made to fight. Even if he won, he believed, he would return to a department whose leadership had already decided it no longer wanted him.

Two days later, after seven years as a Pawtucket police officer, Pichardo resigned.

His letter was brief. Policing, he wrote, had meant a great deal to him and his family, but over the previous three years the department had made clear that he was no longer welcome because of his “philosophical convictions.” Remaining, he wrote, would only bring more grief to him and his family.

He did not apologize for speaking out.

"My only regret," he wrote, "is that I was not articulate and/or diplomatic enough in my attempts to explain my position." On the 18th, he walked the letter to the Office of Professional Standards, shook hands with his coworkers, turned in his badge, firearm, radio, and keys, and left police headquarters for the last time.

Pichardo alleges that the investigations and escalating discipline he was faced with were retaliation for speaking out about Flock. The reality may be more complicated. His union, which had backed him when the department sought to punish him for his comments to the Valley Breeze, says it saw no evidence that the later investigations were retaliatory. They believed another Pawtucket officer who engaged in comparable conduct would have faced similar discipline.

Whether that is true is difficult to establish. Pichardo does not deny that he broke department rules in several of the incidents. His argument is that the rules were enforced differently against him—that conduct that might have earned another officer a warning became an internal inquiry, and misconduct that might otherwise have brought lesser discipline resulted in lengthy unpaid suspensions. He claims he had seen other officers do worse and face less. There is no way to know what would have happened to the version of Pichardo who never called the Valley Breeze.

After resigning, Pichardo spent months trying to remain in law enforcement. He applied to other police departments, private-security jobs, and campus police positions, including one at his alma mater, Salve Regina University. Some never responded. Others interviewed him before deciding not to move forward. An acquaintance who works in campus security at a local college eventually asked around and offered an explanation: "You're blackballed."

He found work instead as a caregiver for a person with intellectual and developmental disabilities.

Pichardo tried to tell himself that he had done enough. But he couldn’t shake the feeling that he had left something unfinished. “My conscience was still haunting me,” he told me. “I just wanted to be able to say I tried.”

So he sat down with a friend who started a YouTube account for Pichardo, and they recorded a video.

Since I started speaking with Pichardo in April, the debate over Flock has spread far beyond Pawtucket. Across the country, cities have fought over whether to keep the cameras, some jurisdictions have canceled contracts or imposed new restrictions, and lawmakers in both Republican- and Democratic-led states have pushed for new limits on how the systems can be used. For Pichardo, there is something distinctly American about the backlash. The country has long attached dreams of freedom and self-determination to the car, a mythology reflected in advertising and even in the names of the vehicles themselves: Explorer, Expedition, Escape, Maverick, Liberty. Americans who agreed on little else could still recognize the promise of the open road—that, for a little while, a person might simply leave and be left alone. To Pichardo, Flock threatened that promise.

“That’s freedom,” Pichardo told me. “The ability to drive somewhere and no one knows where you’re going.”

The video opens with Pichardo sitting alone in a plain room, dressed in a crisp cream-colored shirt, daylight spilling through a nearby window. Looking directly into the camera, he tells viewers that speaking publicly is "one of the strangest things" he has ever done. But, he says, he feels obligated to warn them about a technology that has quietly spread into communities across the country.

"To put it bluntly," he says, "if you own a car, you are now being tracked."

He expected a few hundred people to watch. Hundreds of thousands did.

Within weeks, an email arrived from one of Tucker Carlson's bookers. Pichardo assumed it was a prank; he had never really sought a political audience. He had deleted his social media accounts years ago and had little interest in becoming a pundit. But in mid-July, there he was, spending nearly 20 minutes discussing license plate readers, surveillance, and the meaning of privacy with the former Fox News host. He was explaining Flock to one of the largest audiences in American media, in a video bombastically titled “Whistleblower Reveals the Largest Mass Surveillance Operation in History and the Coming Slave State.”

Podcasters started reaching out, followed by local reporters and The Washington Post. Strangers urged him to run for office. Others told him to build up his YouTube channel, lean into the moment, and turn the audience into a career.

The prospect was not without appeal. Pichardo was still rebuilding his life after losing his job; a large audience might offer money, security, even a new profession. But something about it felt dishonest. “The only reason people know who I am,” he told me, “is because I criticized something.”

He had watched enough people online to recognize what he thought of as a trap. You begin with sincere convictions about serving the public, then you begin tracking an audience, and in time, he says, “you become a parody of what you were before.”

His mind returned, he says, to a passage from the Gospel of Matthew. “What profit is it to a man,” the verse goes, “if he gains the whole world, but loses his own soul?”

entries.title: Best Merino Wool Clothing (2026): Base Layers, Hoodies, Jackets
entries.summary: Merino is one of the best fabrics you can wear. We explain the different blends, what “GSM” means, and how to care for your clothes.
entries.content:
Merino wool is a super fiber that's both natural and highly technical. The best merino wool clothing somehow manages to be comfortable in 95-degree heat, while merino base layers keep you warm well below freezing. Unlike synthetic fibers derived from petroleum, merino wool is renewable.

Merino wool’s versatility means there’s a bewildering array of blends and options. Here are our favorite merino wool products that we've tested by wearing and washing (usually in cold water and hung to dry, although we do machine-dry them just to see what happens) over the course of months and, in some cases, even years. Be sure to also check out our apparel guides, including Best Merino Wool T-Shirts, Best Base Layers, Best Puffer Jackets, Best Hoodies, and Best Hiking Boots.

Updated August 2026: I've added a new section for merino-blend pants and additional everyday wool clothing, and swapped out a few sold-out items for this autumn's new arrivals. I've also updated prices and links throughout.

Why Is Merino Wool So Great?

Merino wool is great because you're borrowing a sheep's ability to keep itself warm or cool based on the temperature, a process often referred to as thermoregulation. If you've only ever worn the sort of itchy wool sweaters your proverbial grandmother supposedly made, you might wonder what all the fuss is. The answer is that Merino sheep have thinner, softer wool, which has evolved to keep them comfortable across a wide range of temperatures and is comfortable to wear next to your skin. Wool is sustainable, too. One sheep can produce 4 to 5 pounds of wool per year. But be aware of merino greenwashing, as the process from sourcing the wool to the end product may still involve chemicals, polluted waters, synthetic fabrics, and other things that increase the carbon footprint. Research a company's methods and claims, as cheaper merino wool may not be as sustainable as marketed.

What Does GSM Mean?

Merino wool comes in different weights, which you will often see listed as “200 GSM” or something similar. GSM refers to grams per square meter, sometimes listed as g/m².) What's important is the scale and where your garment falls on it. At the low end, you have T-shirts and underwear, which are typically 150 GSM, though we have seen some as low as 120 GSM. Generally, anything below 200 GSM will be a good base layer or T-shirt. From 200 to 300 GSM are your mid-layers, and anything above 300 is a heavier garment.

If you're more familiar with synthetic ratings like those often used on fleece, know that, from my experience, about 120 to 160 GSM wool corresponds to 100-weight fleece, 160 to 200 GSM wool roughly matches 200-weight fleece, and 200-plus GSM wool is like 300-weight fleece. In every instance, wool is warmer because it's better at trapping heat, especially in the wind. (That said, there are reasons to go with fleece at times, like how incredibly lightweight it can be.)

What Is Nuyarn?

Nuyarn is a merino wool/synthetic hybrid weave, in which merino wool is wrapped around a nylon core for warmth, lightness, and extra durability. The idea is to get the temperature-regulation benefits of merino while adding some of nylon's longevity. In my experience, Nuyarn mostly works. It's our top pick for base layers, though I find it less necessary in more casual garments, where I prefer 100 percent wool.

How to Care for Merino Wool

Most merino products have care instructions that say to wash them in cold water and lay flat to dry. The latter is important, as hanging wool to dry will stretch it out (because of the water weight). While most merino labels say the garment can be machine washed, my experience has been that hand-washing will extend its life. This is particularly true of very lightweight (150 GSM) merino base layers and T-shirts. The exception is Minus33's Microweight Raglan short-sleeve T-shirt, which is machine-washable and dryer-friendly. Having done both to mine for over a year, I can vouch that it holds up.

I've never had a problem storing merino in my closet between wears, but for long-term storage, I recommend you take precautions against moths, which are notorious for eating holes in wool. I have lost merino garments to moths.

If you don't want the fabric to smell like mothballs, there are better solutions. I make sure to wash and thoroughly dry whatever I am storing, then I seal it in a compression bag. Another option is to put your merino garment in a cotton bag or wrap it in cotton, then put it in a plastic bin. It's very important to make sure that the garment is completely dry before using any of these storage methods; otherwise, your wool will smell musty and moldy. Other options include storing your garment in a cedar chest, a good natural deterrent for moths, or using moth traps or lavender sachets, which will repel moths.

100 Percent Merino vs. Blends

Should you buy 100 percent merino or go for a blend? It depends on the garment in question, the use case, and your preferences. Probably the best way to find out is to try several and see what you like. One advantage of blends is that they're stretchy, which makes them better for active pursuits like hiking, rock climbing, and the like. I like 100 percent merino for heavier mid-layers like hoodies or jackets, but I prefer blends for lighter layers. My experience has been that the closer I get to my skin, the more blend I want, with Nuyarn being my top pick for base layers.

There are also some alpaca blends out there that are wonderfully soft (I love everything I've tried from Paka and Arms of Andes). Alpaca is not merino, but both share similar qualities. If you're one of the rare people who do find merino itchy, you might be allergic to lanolin, which is the skin oil produced by sheep. Alpacas don't make lanolin, and the fibers are thinner and finer than merino. That makes alpaca warmer and softer, but it's also more expensive.

Merino vs. Synthetic Fibers

Synthetic fabrics include polyester, nylon, polypropylene, rayon, or blends of these and other fabrics—everything but cotton, wool, and linen. In most cases, they are less expensive than natural fibers.

Synthetics generally win for wicking away sweat, which means they tend to feel drier. They also usually dry faster, so for things like socks and underwear, even most "merino" options are often more than 50 percent synthetic. Synthetics are just better at handling moisture. How much this matters depends on a host of personal factors. For example, I feel weird and almost clammy in anything synthetic, so I don't really care how much moisture it wicks away.

The downside is that synthetics retain odor. Some chemical treatments can help, but I've never tried anything synthetic that is as odor-resistant as merino wool.

Another difference is breathability. Synthetics are passable in this department, but it's where merino really excels. If you're hot and are hiking up an exposed slope toward an open pass and then dropping down into the cool of a forest, merino is your friend, because the breathability means less sweat to cool you when you get out of the sun. Again, how much this matters depends on your body.

The final factor worth thinking about is durability. In some cases, synthetics will last longer than pure merino, particularly in scenarios where abrasion is a major source of wear. To my mind, this is another reason to choose a merino blend rather than going all the way to synthetics, but it's something to consider if you do a lot of off-trail hiking or rock climbing—any activity where your clothes are going to take a beating.

Base Layers

To really see how remarkable merino wool is, start at the bottom, with the clothes next to your skin. Merino really shines as a base layer. It's warmer for the weight, wicks moisture well, and unlike synthetic fabrics, merino stays stink-free for days of wear. Be sure to read our layering guide for more on how to put it all together and stay comfortable in any weather. We also have a separate guide to the best base layers if you want to know all your options, but here are our top merino picks from that guide.

The Ibex Woolies Pro Tech Crew is the best lightweight merino base layer we've tested. If you want a hard-wearing shirt, this is it. Woolies are Nuyarn (see above), which is 85 percent merino wool and 15 percent nylon—the merino wool is wrapped around a nylon core, which increases the warmth while being lighter (5 oz for the men's large) and more durable. This is my top pick for all things technical. It's what I bring hiking and backpacking, and it's a great pick for running, climbing, and other high-aerobic activities when it’s cold. I also love the Woolies Pro Tech Bottoms, which I bring backpacking in all but the warmest weather.

Aside from comfort and warmth, part of the reason we recommend Woolies is that they last. Ibex is what passes for a heritage company in this space; the company was founded in 1997 and has been cranking out merino garments for a long time. Properly cared for, Woolies will keep you comfortably warm for years to come.

When I want something a bit warmer than the lightweight Woolies above, I reach for Smartwool's Classic long-sleeve base layer. These may be the most popular merino shirts around, and for good reason: They're very comfortable and on the looser side, feature heavy-duty seams that don't rub, and sit off the shoulder for more comfort when wearing a backpack. At 87 percent merino wool (blended with nylon), these are also very durable while remaining lightweight (10.3 oz for a men's large). This Smartwool shirt, along with the matching pants, is great for chilly winter days.

The picks above all have what my wife calls “that sporty look,” which the industry refers to as “technical.” This 100 percent merino shirt from Unbound is the opposite: it just looks like a regular long-sleeve shirt. It's incredibly soft, and while it does pill a bit if you run it through the dryer (don't), it's proven itself plenty durable—I've been wearing it constantly for over a year now, and it still looks like it did when I got it. It's the long-sleeve base-layer twin to our favorite T-shirt (see below). It's on the thin side for a base layer, which makes it perfect for cool-weather mornings in the shoulder seasons. It's versatile too; it can be used as a base layer, but it also works as a T-shirt when it's not too chilly. Fit runs true to size, and if the one you want is sold out, be patient; Unbound frequently updates its stock.

Here are a few more to consider, but really, go read our base layer guide.

Don't forget your neck. I live in this Turtle Fur gaiter during the winter, and I also use the lighter, superfine version for hiking at elevation in the summer to keep the sun off my neck without resorting to sunscreen. It's wonderfully soft, not overly tight, and never smells.

Merino Mid-Layers

Fleece has its place, but I rarely wear it these days. I prefer merino for my mid-layers. It's better at helping your body regulate its temperature. The one place fleece still wins for me is backpacking. It's almost always lighter for comparable warmth, at least in mid-layers.

Like the Northern Lights or the McRib, the thickest Ibex wool hoodie appears irregularly and with some fanfare. The Mammoth Hoodie is a big, furry beast of a garment—basically the weight of the classic American Giant hoodie, but made of 85 percent wool cut with 15 percent nylon for added warmth and stretch. Ibex says it's the warmest hoodie it has ever made, and in my week of testing I've used it in place of a jacket in mid-thirties temps. It has an athletic cut with zippered pockets and thumb holes. I do wear a stocking hat with it in the cold, because the scuba hood is meant to fit under a helmet, which means it's too small to provide enough warmth for my large shaved head on its own. —Martin Cizmar

This very warm hoodie (300 GSM) is 85 percent merino, 12 percent nylon, 3 percent spandex. The synthetics woven in give it plenty of stretch and help with durability. I find this the warmest of all the merino hoodies I've tested at this fabric weight, and it's particularly good at blocking wind. I also like the simple, clean lines of the cut and design. If the Boulder Hoodie is unavailable, check out the Chase, which has the same material content but slightly heavier.

There's a dearth of merino wool for kids. Perhaps the price, for something kids may outgrow in a few months, makes the economics unappealing. Whatever the case, very few companies offer kid-size merino. In fact, this Minus33 hoodie isn't available in child sizes, but the extra-small women's fit my 10-year-old perfectly and still fits her at 11. You'll want to check the size chart on Minus33 for your own kids, but if they do fit, this is a fantastic hoodie. It's plenty warm (and my daughter is always cold) and durable enough to stand up to kid life—climbing trees and running through the woods—and the hand warmers pair well with mittens on cold days. Best of all, when kids are involved, this one can be machine-washed and tumble-dried. It won't shrink or lose its shape, and the colors won't bleed.

A growing number of studies have shown that PFAs—hormone-disrupting chemicals commonly used in many plastics—are found in ordinary sportswear, like leggings and sports bras. If you, like me, are on a quest to replace your polyester clothing with natural fibers, then Ibex’s 100 percent merino wool Shak Jacket is the natural candidate to replace your (my) worn-out Patagonia Better Sweater.

I took this jacket on a recent trip to Ireland. It’s surprisingly dense and soft to the touch. It kept me warm on blustery 30-degree days, layered easily under my rain jacket and over my tank top, and looked sleek enough to go out to dinner. In western Ireland, at least (“I like your jumper!” said many an Irishman). It doesn't pack down quite as compactly as a synthetic layer might, nor is it as light, but it looks much nicer, and it won't feel like slime on your skin when it gets wet. —Adrienne So

Grid fleece is awesome. It's warm for the weight, and very breathable, making it great for highly aerobic activities. Despite all that, I prefer the comfort of merino and bring my merino mid-layers backpacking, even though there's a definite weight penalty. Thanks to Ridge Merino's Cloudripper jacket, though, I can now have my merino and wear my grid fleece, too. Ridge has combined grid fleece with merino wool to give you the advantages of both—keeping the merino against your skin, but using grid fleece to improve ventilation and make the jacket much lighter. The men's large I've been testing weighs just 16.1 ounces on my scale. That's 4 ounces more than Patagonia's R1 Air hoodie, probably the most popular grid fleece jacket out there, but I have found the Cloudripper to be considerably warmer than the Air.

The Cloudripper jackets (there's also a half-zip version and a crew neck version) are made of two fabrics. The first is wool grid fleece (265 GSM), which is 69 percent merino, 15 percent recycled polyester, 13 percent nylon, and 3 percent spandex. The secondary fabric is a grid fleece (180 GSM) that's 51 percent recycled polyester, 41 percent Merino wool, and 8 percent Lycra. The more traditional grid fleece with the higher polyester count is used mainly on the hood and lower back, while everything that would touch your skin (if you don't have a base layer on) is merino.

I've been testing the full zip Cloudripper for about a month now, and it's quickly become my go-to mid-layer on the cool fall mornings and evenings that have settled in where I live. It's proven itself on some early morning bike rides, where it strikes a balance between keeping me warm when I'm first starting out, and venting off the excess heat I'm generating once I get going. It also doesn't get stinky like my purely polyester grid fleece. It's the best of grid fleece, married to the best of merino wool, to create what might be the ultimate technical mid-layer.

If you have concerns about using goose down jackets as an insulation layer, merino wool is a decent substitute for synthetic insulation. Vests are like the cheat code of layering if you want to keep your core warm but your arms mobile, or add an extra soupçon of warmth without too much bulk. I like to layer Ibex's Wool Aire Vest under my regular wool coat or rain shell, if I'm going out for the night or on a long run. —Adrienne So

Best Merino Wool T-Shirts

Wool might not seem like a good choice for a summer T-shirt, but merino is surprisingly comfortable even when it's warm. To a point, anyway. On humid days over about 90 degrees Fahrenheit, I usually go with cotton or linen, but anything under 90, and I'm wearing merino. There are a ton of merino T-shirts out there, so many in fact that we now have a guide dedicated to just the best merino T-shirts. Here are our favorites from that guide.

Huckberry's Proof-brand 72-hour Merino T-Shirt is my favorite all-around merino tee. The cut and style are not overly sporty, making it more versatile than a more technical tee. It's an incredibly soft T-shirt, thanks to the 150 GSM weave of superfine merino wool (16.5 micron). It's a blend—87 percent merino and 13 percent nylon—which gives it some stretch, with the trade-off that it will start smelling sooner than a 100 percent merino T-shirt. In the year or so I've been wearing it, I've found the name accurate. You can get about three days out of it before it needs a wash (depending on ambient temps and what you're doing).

I really like that this shirt comes in a wide variety of colors, more than any other shirt I've tested. Proof uses the exact same fabric to make long-sleeve tees, as well as polos and henleys, if you're looking for something more than a T-shirt.

OK, but what about when you do want a more technical cut, with flatlock stitching and offset seams? When I'm hiking, backpacking, paddleboarding, or doing just about anything outdoors, this is the T-shirt I reach for first. The jersey knit is lightweight (84 percent 145-GSM merino, 16 percent synthetic), soft, and comfortable—not too hot in the sun (it also has a UPF rating of 20), warm enough when it's cool. It's also durable (I've been rolling jiujitsu in this shirt for years and it's fine) and machine washable. You can even throw it in the dryer; no need to baby this T-shirt.

As I say in our guide to the best merino T-shirts, if I could have only one merino T-shirt, it would be this one. It's the softest, most luxurious merino shirt I've tested. It's 95 percent merino wool, meaning it can go quite a while before it smells, and it's great when you want to travel light—bring two of these, and that's all you need in half the world. Did I mention how soft this is? It reminds me more of cashmere than merino. Taylor Stitch says that’s because it uses a mercerization process on its wool. Whatever the case, it is soft. Very, very soft. My only real gripe here is the very limited color selection. Taylor Stitch typically has a heather blue and heather black available all the time, and every now and then some other colors will be available on a very limited basis.

Unbound Merino's T-shirt has long been a favorite of WIRED readers, and it's also long been a favorite of travelers. It's very soft, and because it's 100 percent merino wool, it'll stay odor-free longer than any blended shirt. It's also lightweight and packs down to a tiny roll, which is perfect if you're looking to simplify down to one bag (really, is there any other way to travel?). I love how soft these shirts are, and they dry faster than any merino T-shirt I've tested.

Ibex's Goat short-sleeve crew differs from my previous favorite active merino wool T-shirt, the Artilect Utilitee. The sizing is quite a bit looser, which makes it a little harder to wear while layering or underneath a climbing harness. The wool blend is also higher—89 percent 150 GSM merino wool, compared to the Utilitee's 60 percent—so it's much softer and way less stretchy. However, it's still shockingly versatile and keeps me warm in the shade while ventilating sweat once I get above the tree line. —Adrienne So

Best Merino Sweaters

Forget what you know about the scratchy wool sweaters of yore. When you need something heavier, try the merino version of this tried-and-true cold weather garment. They're warm, soft, and don't itch.

Finisterre pulls its name from a North Atlantic headland, from the Latin "Finis Terrae," roughly the "end of the Earth." I had to replace the Furlong sweater from this guide as Finisterre isn't making it anymore, but luckily the Barents sweater is also an incredibly warm, awesome wool sweater. It's made of 70 percent recycled wool and feels heavy, like an old fisherman's sweater—a fisherman from the end of the Earth, that is. Indeed, this is a very heavy sweater that I mainly reserve for the coldest of days, but when you need it, the Barents is there for you.

OK, so this is alpaca fiber, not merino wool. Technically, it's 65 percent royal alpaca fiber and 35 percent recycled nylon. Like merino wool, this textile cousin offers natural thermoregulation, keeping you comfortable across a broad range of temps. It also has similar odor-resistant properties. In the end, what I love about this sweater is less the technical abilities (though those are great) and more just that it's very soft and comfortable. This sweater is lightweight (about 15 ounces), but warm. It works well layered under a jacket, or on its own, and it comes in a wide range of colors.

The Best Merino Pants

Wool pants really gave me pause the first time I heard the phrase, but nothing I've tested has been the least bit itchy or weird. In fact, both pants I recommend below are among the lightest and softest I own.

Unbound Merino's travel pants are a light, comfortable merino blend with plenty of stretch and freedom of movement, thanks to the 5 percent elastane. As you would expect from anything Unbound makes, these pack down fantastically small. Serious travelers take note: You can pack two pairs of these for every pair of jeans. The only downside is that the pants are on the thin side, so you won't want to wear them on their own in cold climates. But grab a nice merino base layer from the recommendations above, throw it on under these pants, and you'll be fine in all but the coldest of conditions.

These have a more formal look than some merino pants I've tried, making them potentially more versatile. You might be able to pull off going to the office wearing them, depending on your company's dress code and how far your boss's definition of “business casual” stretches. I've worn them to nice restaurants without a second look, and yet they don't scream “I've got money” when you're stumbling back to your hotel room at 2 am.

Huckberry's Proof 72-hour merino pants are frustratingly close to being the perfect pants for travel and anything else. Their only downfall is that the merino count is pretty low, just 47 percent, which ends up making these feel more synthetic (which, my mathematically inclined friends, they are). That's not necessarily a bad thing; they're still comfortable and perform pretty well, though obviously with the high polyester count they won't go nearly as long as a higher merino blend. But they're comfortable, plenty stretchy (you can work out in them in a pinch), and they're a more relaxed, casual look than the Unbound pants above. Still, every time I wear them I can't help thinking, what would these be like at 75 percent merino? My guess is they'd be even better.

Socks, Underwear, and Bras

You could argue this is the true base layer, but we'll skip that and just say that merino wool underwear, socks, and bras are so much nicer than their synthetic counterparts. The caveat is that while merino wool is very soft, most products in this category are blends, usually with some form of nylon. Still, if you haven't tried merino underwear yet, you're in for a treat. After testing dozens of each, these are our favorites.

Darn Tough socks are a WIRED favorite. They're great for skiing, hiking, climbing, and just about anything else you want to do. These blends vary by weight, but most are around 50 percent nylon and 50 percent merino, which makes them dry a bit faster than pure merino while staying plenty warm and comfortable. Darn Tough's socks also last. Mine are going on two years now, with no worn areas or holes in sight. If you do develop holes, Darn Tough socks come with an unconditional lifetime guarantee. You can return them for another pair, no receipt needed, which is kind of crazy if you consider the abuse that hiking socks take.

Minus33 socks are my personal favorite merino socks. I have several pairs of the lightweight and midweight, and even one pair of the expedition, though those are so thick and warm I rarely wear them (they're perfect when the temps drop below zero, though). My favorite are the Lightweight Mountain Heritage Boot Wool Socks, which are perfect for hiking or wearing around town. Minus33 doesn't publish a blend breakdown for these, but I would guess they're about 60/40 wool to nylon, with plenty of softness and stretch.

The phrase “wool underwear” might conjure images of some lumberjack from the 1800s with hair growing through the weaves of his itchy, hot long johns, but that's not what the merino underwear we've tested is like. In most cases, these are blends, usually with nylon.

Wool&Prince’s 6.5-inch wool boxers are the softest, most comfortable merino boxers I've tested. These are the best merino boxers for a very simple reason: they don't ride up when you move. Why? Because the weave on the legs runs vertically, the fabric stretches without riding up. These boxers stayed put while I did squats and lunges, climbed stairs, and rolled juijitsu. I also like that the merino content is quite high (for boxers) at 75 percent (the remainder is 22 percent nylon and 3 percent spandex), and the 250-GSM fabric strikes a nice balance: durable but not so heavy you can't wear it in the heat.

These are the only 100 percent merino underwear I've tested (there's elastic in the waistband, but it's surrounded by wool), and they're also some of my favorites, especially in cold weather. These are longer than any of the other boxers I've tried. They are rated 170 GSM, making them a little lighter, but because their merino content is higher, these are the warmest I've tested. After years of testing merino underwear, these are my favorite on all but the hottest days.

Women's merino underwear is really difficult to do well. If it's thin and stretchy enough to be comfortable, then it tends to warp and stretch in the washing machine (I do air-dry my clothes, but you should be able to toss your underwear in a washing machine and have it last). This, sadly, was the fate of the pairs of Ibex and Wool& underwear that I tried. They shrank and warped instantly, despite drying on the line.

Of the other pairs that I've tried, the two best are Branwyn's underwear and Unbound. Unbound's underwear is a 60 percent merino, 34 percent nylon, and 6 percent Spandex blend at a rather impressive 290 GSM. It's durable enough to survive being washed (I did line-dry them) and comfortable enough to wear under my clothes (though there are no circumstances under which I would consider a wool thong comfortable). —Adrienne So

Branwyn makes what they call merino wool performance sets. I am a fan of Branwyn’s clothes, all of which are Oeko-Tex 100 certified, which means every component of the clothing has been independently tested against a list of up to 350 toxic chemicals. This is one of the most widely known and respected labels for consumer safety. These fit true to size. (I suppose it’s important to note here that I’m a small-busted woman, and that Branwyn makes a Busty Bra if you need more support.)

However, this isn't quite supportive enough for running, which is why Branwyn launched the Racerback Bra. It's pretty impressive that Branwyn made merino wool compressive enough for medium-impact activity. I like that it offers full coverage, with no annoying small and twisty straps and no padding. It precludes the need to change from cotton “everyday” underwear to tight nylon “sport” underwear every time I want to do something active, which is all the time. —Adrienne So

The Best Everyday Merino Clothes

I'll confess that when I launched this guide years ago, I thought of merino wool mainly as an outdoor-related fabric. It is great for that, but I've since discovered that merino is good for everything, especially travel, since it can be worn several times without any odors. I've tried merino pants, dress shirts, workout clothes, hats, and more. The best stuff I've tested is below.

Proper Cloth's Reda dress shirt is one of the nicest things I've ever tested. The photographs really don't do justice to how good this shirt looks in person. As you would expect from merino, the Reda is nicely breathable, much lighter and more breathable than your typical dress shirt. I found it quite comfortable even in the summer humidity. The Reda fabric is thin, though, with moisture-wicking, which means you do see some armpit sweat when it's warm. The good news is, of course, it won't retain any smells.

I strongly suggest babying this one a little bit. I machine-washed it cold and laid it flat to dry (which was quite quick), but you'll likely want to give it a light pressing to get it wrinkle-free. If you're traveling, packing these down will get you a few wrinkles, but it's nothing you can't get out pretty quickly. The big question I had going in was, how durable will this be? Given the thin fabric and the sometimes fragile nature of merino when spun this fine, I expected obvious signs of wear pretty quickly. Fortunately, I was wrong. More than three months of steady use now has done nothing to this shirt, and it looks as good as the day I got it.

This button-up, long-sleeve shirt from Woolly is much more casual than the Proper Cloth shirt above. It's more what you might call business casual. It's comfortable, soft, well-made, and has the 100 percent merino advantage of being odor-resistant. The only thing I am not quite so fond of is the slightly shimmery look, but that's just personal preference.

These super comfy, casual sweatpants from Ridge Merino are some of the most comfortable pants I've ever worn. I don't often work out in them; I've never actually “yogged” in them, but they're great around the house. These are 100 percent merino wool (275 GSM) with what Ridge calls a terry fabric (they feel like sweatpants).

This wool skirt turned out to be a summer favorite for our tester. She says it's light enough to pair with a T-shirt in all but the hottest of weather, but not so light that it's see-through when you're backlit. An A-line skirt, it falls just below the knee and features two front pockets. It's a blend of 85 percent merino, with 12 percent nylon and 3 percent Spandex for a little stretch. Woolx calls this blend DuraLite, and while it's different, in my experience with the company's T-shirts, it's very much like NuYarn and other blends, with merino spun around the nylon core for extra strength and durability.

entries.title: The Powerful Chinese AI Model Experts Warned About Is Here
entries.summary: Z.ai’s latest AI model release could help companies secure their systems—or find its way into the hands of hackers.
entries.content:
It’s now even easier to find—and exploit—vulnerabilities in computer systems using AI.

Last Friday, the Chinese AI company Z.ai announced a powerful open-weight model that it says is capable of automating cutting-edge coding and cybersecurity tasks almost as well as the best publicly available models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

The new model, GLM 5.3, could be a gift for companies looking to secure their systems against attacks, providing a cheaper way to scan for hidden bugs and other weaknesses. Open-weight—or free-to-download—models can be run on one’s own hardware and are often significantly less costly than closed models like Claude and GPT. Alongside the new model, Z.ai released OpenVuln, a service for scanning code repositories for vulnerabilities using GLM 5.3.

For now, the new model is in a limited release with trusted partners, but it shows how quickly open-weight models are gaining superhuman hacking skills. And that might pose problems if the model is harnessed by criminals and other bad actors.

That prospect is especially sobering following a string of startling incidents involving rogue AI agents with advanced cyber-skills. In recent weeks, OpenAI, Anthropic, and independent security researchers have revealed examples of agents escaping from testing environments and autonomously hacking into outside systems, including the research platform Hugging Face, to complete tasks.

On Monday, OpenAI president Greg Brockman warned in a blog post that the Hugging Face incident would go down as “a watershed moment for cybersecurity because it gave a peek into how the capabilities of a typical threat actor will evolve in upcoming months.”

Brockman argued that AI models are becoming so good at scouring codebases for unknown flaws and analyzing systems for misconfigurations that it’s crucial for organizations to use AI to scan their systems and identify issues before they can be exploited.

OpenAI would, of course, like companies to use its AI to do that. So far, it’s moving carefully in providing access to its most capable AI. Like Anthropic, OpenAI has made its most advanced models available to a limited number of partners prior to full release. The US government is also wrestling with the issue and now reviews frontier models as part of their releases.

Some believe that open-source AI will be crucial to shoring systems up from attack; Nvidia recently announced an alliance to promote the use of open AI for cybersecurity. A previous version of Z.ai’s GLM was used by Hugging Face to shore up its systems after an unreleased OpenAI model went rogue and broke them last month.

In a post on X, Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, a web design and hosting company, said his engineers had tested GLM 5.3 as a tool for scanning sites for bugs. “Given its lower costs, I expect this to be a boon for defensive security work,” Rauch wrote in his post. “It’s the new open frontier.”

Z.ai said in a post announcing GLM 5.3 that it had improved the model by “post-training,” which involves giving a model examples of solved problems and letting it learn through experimentation. The company cited coding and cybersecurity benchmark scores that show GLM 5.3 nearing or even exceeding the scores of Anthropic and OpenAI’s models in some cases, like one popular cybersecurity benchmark called CyberGym.

Z.ai also acknowledged the risk of releasing powerful open models in its post. “These capabilities can help defenders identify weaknesses earlier, validate risks, and accelerate remediation,” the company wrote. “They also create clear dual-use risks. We are therefore taking a staged approach to release. Selected security partners will first evaluate GLM-5.3 in controlled settings.” Z.ai says that full access to the model will be available in two weeks.

“This model looks exceptional, with a somewhat astounding increase in scores,” Nathan Lambert, a prominent AI expert, wrote in a post about GLM 5.3. “This is another step towards the inevitable proliferation of very strong cyber capabilities across the economy.”

Z.ai’s latest release also highlights China’s edge in open-weight models. Although the US has sought to restrict the country’s access to the most advanced chips for training AI models, recent months have seen the release of several extremely powerful open-weight models, including Qwen 3.8 Max from Alibaba and Kimi 3 from Moonshot AI. Z.ai has previously said that it used Chinese-made chips from Huawei to train some of its models. Meta, which appeared to have abandoned open-source AI, now seems poised to lead the US challenge with a powerful model called Muse Spark.

The US government is developing a framework designed to mitigate the impact of AI’s advancing cyber capabilities. A big remaining question is what it should do with open models—especially as they introduce more potential risk.
